Senses.Note: Family check: “clap the hands” (撫掌), “hand-clapping” (拍手撫掌), “clap and laugh loudly” (撫掌大笑), “clap once” (撫掌一下), and “clap three times” (撫掌三下) all denote the same physical action. They differ in accompanying speech and count, not referent, so they remain one sense.

Senses.Explanation: Clapping the hands is a narrated audible gesture, often paired with laughter or used to close a comment. The gesture occurs 746 times in 231 allowlisted texts, commonly as a visible turn in a public exchange. It may stand alone (‘clapped three times’), accompany departure, a shout, or a blow, or join laughter: ‘clapped his hands and laughed loudly’ occurs 98 times in 60 texts. The record does not assign one fixed attitude to it. Yangqi Fanghui claps and laughs before saying an answer is ‘not worth half a cent’; another monk claps once after shouting; Xiyuan claps three times when asked why he bathes without an attendant. Caoshan later explicitly calls the action ‘hand-clapping’ and distinguishes Xiyuan’s use from the same physical action elsewhere. In the Shuilao case, Shuilao rises after Mazu kicks him, claps and laughs, and speaks; later records repeatedly cite that sequence. Zen bends an ordinary gesture by making it an answer, rejoinder, appraisal, or recorded public-interview move, while the surrounding words—not the gesture alone—establish whether a given occurrence is laughter, challenge, celebration, or dismissal.
